questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This probes understanding of durability semantics in buffered I/O with journaling filesystems, including the roles of the page cache, journal commits, and barriers. It also checks practical mitigation strategies.

## Key Concepts

- Data vs metadata flush semantics and barriers
- Journal commit ordering and writeback paths
- fdatasync, fsync, and O_SYNC tradeoffs in throughput vs durability

## Code Example

```javascript
// Pseudocode: durability after write
const n = write(fd, buf, len);
if (n === len) {
  fdatasync(fd);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test durability guarantees under simulated crashes?
- Compare fdatasync vs O_SYNC in a high-throughput server and discuss performance implications.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of per-core data locality, lock-free synchronization, and work-stealing basics in a beginner-friendly OS context. 

## Key Concepts
- Per-core queues and locality
- Work-stealing and fairness
- Lock-free CAS and memory barriers
- False sharing considerations

## Code Example
```c
// Minimal sketch (pseudo-code)
typedef struct { volatile int head, tail; Task* buf[CAP]; } Deque;
void push(Deque* d, Task* t){ int i = atomic_fetch_add(&d->tail, 1); d->buf[i % CAP] = t; }
Task* pop(Deque* d){ int t = --d->tail; if (t >= d->head) return d->buf[t % CAP]; return NULL; }
Task* steal(Deque* nd){ // neighbor's deque; atomically take half
  int h = nd->head; int t = nd->tail; if (h >= t) return NULL; Task* s = nd->buf[h % CAP]; nd->head = h+1; return s; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test starvation? 
- How would you extend to dynamic capacity and NUMA-awareness?
